Central Nervous System
Physiology
Thalamus, Hypothalamus, Limbic system, RF
At a glance

The thalamus, reticular formation, hypothalamus and limbic system are subcortical centers that relay sensation, control tone and arousal, regulate visceral and endocrine functions, and shape behavior and memory.

Thalamus

Functional structure

  • Two thalami, one in each cerebral hemisphere; each is an almond-shaped mass of grey matter about 4 cm long, lying along the lateral wall of the third ventricle.
  • Bounded by the internal capsule and lentiform nucleus, and superiorly and laterally by the caudate nucleus.
  • Its posterior extension is the pulvinar (neothalamus).
  • It is the largest part of the diencephalon and the highest subcortical center for sensory functions.
  • A T-shaped sheet of white fibers, the internal medullary lamina, divides it into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups.

Physiological classification of thalamic nuclei

Non-specific projection nuclei

  • Midline and intralaminar nuclei.
  • Diffuse to all areas of the cerebral cortex, the basal ganglia and neighboring thalamic nuclei.

Specific projection nuclei

  • Discharge to specific cortical areas and other brain centers.
  • Listed in the table below.
NucleusInputProjection / function
Posteroventral lateral (PVLNT)Spinal and medial lemnisciSensory areas 3,1,2 and 5,7
Posteroventral medial (PVMNT)Trigeminal lemniscusSensory areas 3,1,2 and 5,7
Lateral ventralNeocerebellumMotor areas 4 and 6; shares in motor control of the basal ganglia
Lateral geniculate body (LGB)Visual impulses from the two corresponding halves of both retinaeOccipital area 17 around the calcarine fissure
Medial geniculate body (MGB)Auditory impulses from both earsTemporal auditory area 41
Anterior nucleiMammillary body of hypothalamusLink to limbic system: emotional behaviors, recent memories, autonomic reactions
Dorsal (dorsomedial, dorsolateral)–Frontal association areas
Pulvinar–Parietal, temporal and occipital lobes; integrates somatic, visual and auditory sensations

Reticular Formation (RF)

Functional structure

  • Millions of neurons spread along the mid-ventral part of the whole brainstem.
  • Corresponds to the spinal cord interneurons and is continuous with them in the upper cervical segments.
  • Extends upward to the intralaminar and non-specific thalamic nuclei, then diffuses to nearly all cortical areas.

Types of neurons

1) Sensory neurons

Largest in number but smallest in size, with short axons and many interconnections. They are sites of convergence, divergence and reverberating circuits, and link lower and higher centers. They receive impulses from:

  • All ascending tracts, including auditory, olfactory and visual pathways.
  • Higher centers: cerebral cortex, hypothalamus, basal ganglia, cerebellum and vestibular apparatus.

2) Motor neurons

Fewer but larger, with longer axons, forming two fiber types:

  • Ascending fibers: connect first with non-specific thalamic nuclei, then diffuse to nearly all cortex, forming the reticular activating system (RAS).
  • Descending fibers: reach alpha and gamma anterior horn cells at all spinal levels as the reticulospinal tracts, which regulate muscle tone.

3) Specific centers

Collections of neurons with defined functions, e.g. red nucleus, olivary nuclei, vestibular nuclei, respiratory centers, vasomotor and cardiac centers, deglutition and vomiting centers.

4) Neurotransmitter-secreting neurons

Serotonergic, noradrenergic, adrenergic, dopaminergic and opioid-secreting neurons regulate the chemistry of the brain.

Functions

  • Link between higher brain centers and lower spinal centers.
  • Regulation of muscle tone (facilitatory and inhibitory parts, below).
  • Contains respiratory, cardiovascular and vasomotor centers, so regulates most autonomic functions.
  • Arousal, through the reticular activating system.
  • Pain perception and control: many opiate receptors and neurons secreting endogenous enkephalins and endorphins.
  • Regulation of brain chemistry.

Control of muscle tone

Facilitatory RF

  • Dorsolateral reticular formation in the pons.
  • Has its own intrinsic activity.
  • Stimulated by area 4, neocerebellum and vestibular nucleus; inhibited by suppressor cortical centers.
  • Gives the ventral reticulospinal tract, which increases muscle tone.

Inhibitory RF

  • Ventromedial reticular formation in the medulla.
  • No intrinsic activity.
  • Stimulated by suppressor cortical areas, basal ganglia and paleocerebellum.
  • Gives the lateral reticulospinal tract, which decreases muscle tone.

Hypothalamus

Nuclei

  • Anterior group: supraoptic, preoptic, paraventricular.
  • Medial group: tuber cinereum, dorsomedial, ventromedial.
  • Lateral group: lateral part of tuber cinereum, lateral nuclei.
  • Posterior group: mammillary body, posterior nuclei.

Connections

  • Afferent from: limbic system, basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem centers (middle raphe nuclei) and all ascending tracts.
  • Efferent to: pituitary gland, limbic system, thalamus and brainstem centers (respiratory, vasomotor, cardiac).

Functions

  • Blood glucose and feeding behavior (glucoreceptors); body temperature (thermoreceptors); water and electrolyte balance (osmoreceptors); thirst and water intake.
  • Endocrine control: releasing and inhibitory factors to the anterior pituitary through the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal circulation; ADH and oxytocin through the hypothalamo-hypophyseal neural tract to the posterior pituitary; a nervous connection to the adrenaline-secreting medullary center and then the suprarenal medulla.
  • Higher center of the autonomic nervous system, controlling many visceral functions.
  • Emotional and behavioral activity through limbic connections.
  • Sleep-wakefulness mechanism and pain control systems.

Limbic System

Anatomy and physiology

Anatomically, it is the rim of cortical tissue encircling the corpus callosum: orbital surface of the frontal lobe, subcallosal and cingulate gyri, parahippocampal gyrus, uncus and pyriform nucleus, plus associated nuclei (septal nuclei, amygdala).

Definition

Physiologically, the limbic system is the part of the brain regulating vegetative functions: behavior, body temperature, osmolality, drive to eat and drink, sexual behavior and olfaction. The hypothalamus is one of its central elements.

Characteristic features

  • Many interconnections between its nuclei.
  • The Papez circuit connects limbic system, thalamus and hypothalamus.
  • Many reverberating circuits, giving prolonged after discharge.
  • Few connections with the neocortex.

Functions

  • Olfaction: specific reactions to specific odors.
  • Behavioral changes: cognition (awareness of the sensation and its cause), affect (pleasant or unpleasant feeling) and conation (urge to act, with changes such as heart rate and blood pressure).
  • Sexual behavior: desire and integration of reflexes leading to erection, mating and ejaculation.
  • Feeding behavior: appetite for types of food (quality rather than quantity).
  • Learning: through regulation of conditioned reflexes.
  • Short-acting memory: reverberating circuits are its basic mechanism.
  • Via the hypothalamus: secretion of some hormones (regulating Na+ and K+ levels, catecholamines) and autonomic reactions accompanying sensations.

Check yourself

Which nuclei of the thalamus diffuse to all cortical areas?

The non-specific midline and intralaminar nuclei.

What forms the reticular activating system?

The ascending fibers of RF motor neurons, which connect with non-specific thalamic nuclei and then diffuse to nearly all cortex.

Which circuit connects the limbic system, thalamus and hypothalamus?

The Papez circuit.

Key Points / Quick Review

Thalamus

  • Highest subcortical sensory center; divided by the internal medullary lamina.
  • Non-specific nuclei (midline, intralaminar) project diffusely.
  • Specific nuclei: PVLNT and PVMNT to areas 3,1,2 and 5,7; LGB to area 17; MGB to area 41; lateral ventral to areas 4 and 6.

Reticular formation

  • Sensory, motor, specific-center and transmitter-secreting neurons.
  • Ascending fibers form the RAS; descending fibers form reticulospinal tracts.
  • Dorsolateral pontine RF facilitates tone; ventromedial medullary RF inhibits it.

Hypothalamus

  • Four nuclear groups: anterior, medial, lateral, posterior.
  • Regulates glucose, temperature, water balance, thirst and pituitary function.
  • Higher autonomic center; sleep-wakefulness and pain control.

Limbic system

  • Cortical rim around the corpus callosum plus septal nuclei and amygdala.
  • Papez circuit, reverberating circuits, few neocortical connections.
  • Olfaction, cognition/affect/conation, sexual and feeding behavior, learning, short-acting memory.
